summary.text: The Haber process is the main industrial method for making ammonia, combining nitrogen from the air with hydrogen over an iron catalyst.
Most of the ammonia is used to make nitrogen fertilizer, either directly or as ammonium nitrate and urea.
Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed it in the first decade of the 20th century, and it now uses 1–2% of the world's energy.

facts.label: Developed by
facts.value: German chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch

facts.label: Conversion per pass
facts.value: About 15% of the gases become ammonia

items.prompt: Only about 15% of the gases turn into ammonia on each pass through the reactor. What does the plant do with the rest?

options.label: It vents them into the air and starts again with new gas
It feeds the unused gases back in, after cooling and removing the ammonia as a liquid
It burns them to power the next pass
It stores them until the plant is shut down

items.explain: The ammonia is cooled and removed as a liquid, and the unused gases are fed back into the reactor.

items.prompt: Air is mostly nitrogen, yet it is hard to turn that nitrogen into compounds. Why?

options.label: Nitrogen in air is too scarce to collect in useful amounts
Nitrogen is too reactive and burns up before it can be used
Nitrogen refuses to stick to any metal surface
Nitrogen is exceptionally stable and its atoms are held by a very strong triple bond

items.explain: Atmospheric nitrogen is abundant but does not readily react with other chemicals, because its two atoms are joined by a very strong triple bond.

items.prompt: Nitrogen and hydrogen stick to an iron surface and then react step by step. Which step sets the speed of the whole process?

options.label: Breaking the strong bond between the two nitrogen atoms
Sticking of the hydrogen to the iron surface
Adding the last hydrogen atom to make ammonia
Letting the finished ammonia leave the surface

items.explain: Breaking the triple bond between the nitrogen atoms is the slowest step, so it controls the speed of the whole process.

items.prompt: How does the iron surface make it possible to break the strong nitrogen bond?

options.label: It heats the gases far above the temperature of the reactor
It removes the hydrogen so nitrogen reacts alone
Bonding to the surface releases enough energy to make that step possible
It slows the nitrogen down so the bond relaxes

items.explain: Bonding to the catalyst surface releases enough energy to make the bond-breaking step possible.

items.prompt: Germany's access to imported nitrates was blocked in World War I. Why did the Haber process matter then?

options.label: It let Germany make cheap fertilizer for soldiers' food
It let Germany make nitric acid for explosives that it could no longer import
It let Germany mine the Chilean deposits in secret
It let Germany heat its factories without coal

items.explain: The process was used to make nitric acid for explosives, which Germany could not import because of the Allied blockade.

items.prompt: At the start of the 20th century, why did researchers step up the search for new sources of ammonia?

options.label: Ammonia had just been found to be toxic in fertilizer
The mined supplies had suddenly become too cheap to bother with
The mined supplies, such as niter and guano, were thought insufficient for future demand
Nitrogen had been found to be missing from the air

items.explain: Demand for nitrates and ammonia was rising, and the main mined sources were thought insufficient to satisfy it.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The Haber process, which also goes by the name Haber–Bosch, is the main way industry makes ammonia, NH₃. It joins nitrogen taken from the air with hydrogen, using an iron catalyst. Most of the ammonia becomes nitrogen fertilizer, used directly or turned into ammonium nitrate and urea.

paragraphs.heading: Why it was needed
paragraphs.text: Through the 19th century, demand for nitrates and ammonia grew fast, both for fertilizers that give plants extra nitrogen and as raw material for industry. Most of the supply came from mined niter deposits and from guano on tropical islands. By the early 1900s, those reserves were thought too small for future needs. Nitrogen gas makes up about 78% of the air, but it is extremely stable and does not easily react with other chemicals.

paragraphs.heading: From lab bench to factory
paragraphs.text: Haber and his assistant Robert Le Rossignol built the high-pressure equipment and catalysts to show the process at laboratory scale. In the summer of 1909 they made ammonia from air, drop by drop, at about 125 mL an hour. The chemical company BASF bought the process and gave Carl Bosch the job of scaling it up. The first industrial plant opened at Oppau in 1913 and was making 20 tonnes a day by 1914. The Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Haber in 1918 and to Bosch in 1931.

paragraphs.heading: On the catalyst surface
paragraphs.text: Nitrogen and hydrogen first stick, or adsorb, to the surface of the solid catalyst. The two atoms in each nitrogen molecule are held by a very strong triple bond, which has to break before anything else can happen. That is the slowest step, so it sets the pace for the whole process, and the energy released by bonding to the surface makes it possible. The nitrogen atoms then gain hydrogen one at a time, becoming NH, then NH₂, then NH₃, which leaves as ammonia gas.

paragraphs.heading: Pressure, heat and recycling
paragraphs.text: The reaction needs both high pressure and high temperature, and most plants still run near the original conditions of 20 MPa and 500 °C. Each trip through the reactor turns only about 15% of the gas into ammonia. So that ammonia is cooled and drawn off as a liquid, and the leftover gases are sent through again.

paragraphs.heading: War and a cheaper catalyst
paragraphs.text: In World War I, the Allied blockade stopped Germany importing what it needed, so it used the process to make nitric acid for explosives. The process was so central to the German war effort that Germany is thought almost certain to have lost within months without it. The first reaction chambers used osmium as the catalyst, which was available only in tiny amounts. In 1909, Alwin Mittasch at BASF found a much cheaper iron-based catalyst that is still used.

paragraphs.heading: The cost today
paragraphs.text: About 230 million tonnes of ammonia came out of the process in 2018. Most of its hydrogen comes from natural gas. Counting the energy to make that hydrogen and purified nitrogen, ammonia production takes 1–2% of the world's energy and 3% to 5% of its natural gas, and it gives off about 3% of all carbon emissions.
